name: Hana's ears and sleep after a concert

parameters.label: Loudness by the speakers
parameters.explain: Concerts reach 94–110 dBA. Sounds at or below 70 are unlikely to harm hearing; long exposure above 85 can.

parameters.label: Hours at the concert
parameters.explain: For every 3 dB louder, the safe time halves — so time and loudness work together.

parameters.label: Distance from the speakers

parameters.explain: Earplugs block part of the sound before it reaches the inner ear.

parameters.label: Hours of sleep

overlay.caption: loud sound tires hair cells · short sleep tires the brain

explain.summary: Hana has two separate problems. Her ears: three hours at about 105 dB is many times a safe day's sound dose, so the tiny hair cells in her inner ear are worn out — that's the ringing and muffled hearing, which usually clears in 16–48 hours. Her brain: five and a half hours of sleep, when teens need 8–10, leaves her unable to focus. Leila's earplugs fixed the first problem, but not the second.
rules: Sound dose = time at the concert compared with the safe time for that loudness (85 dB for 8 hours; half the time for every 3 dB louder).
Moving back halves the energy reaching you: about 6 dB less per doubling of distance. Earplugs block more.
Hair cells tire more as the dose climbs; tired hair cells ring and hear less, and recover over about 16–48 hours.
Focus falls with every hour of sleep she's short of what she needs.

source.fact: Sounds at or below 70 dBA are unlikely to harm hearing; long or repeated exposure at 85 dBA and above can; concerts reach 94–110 dBA.
A temporary hearing loss after loud noise can disappear 16 to 48 hours later; damaged hair cells don't grow back.
The recommended limit is 85 dBA over 8 hours, and every 3 dB louder halves the allowed time (100 dBA: 15 minutes).
Doubling your distance from a sound source lowers the level by about 6 dB.
Teens need 8 to 10 hours of sleep; sleep-deficient people react more slowly and have trouble focusing.
Sleep deficiency causes problems with learning, focusing and reacting.

choice.why: Real earplugs vary — the label's noise reduction rating tells you how much; 20 dB is a typical teaching value.

choice.what: Fatigue rises toward 10 as the dose climbs past a few hundred percent
choice.why: There's no single number linking dose to how tired hair cells get; the curve shows 'more dose, more fatigue'.

choice.what: A workplace limit is used for a concert
choice.why: Workplace limits were made for adults over a working day; they're used here as a yardstick, not a rule.

choice.what: Recovery time grows with fatigue inside the 16–48 hour range
choice.why: The real recovery time varies from person to person.

illustrative: Hana's 105 dB, three hours, 5.5 hours of sleep and the 0–10 scales are made up for a fictional story.

citations.title: Noise-Induced Hearing Loss
citations.supports: Sounds at or below 70 dBA are unlikely to harm hearing; long or repeated exposure at 85 dBA and above can; concerts reach 94–110 dBA; a temporary hearing loss can disappear 16 to 48 hours later; damaged inner-ear hair cells don't grow back; wear earplugs at loud events.

citations.title: Understanding Noise Exposure Limits: Occupational vs. General Environmental Noise
citations.supports: NIOSH's recommended limit is 85 dBA averaged over 8 hours; for every 3 dB louder the allowed time halves (88 dBA 4 h, 94 dBA 1 h, 100 dBA 15 min).

citations.title: Basic Acoustics: the inverse square law
citations.supports: Where the inverse square law holds, each doubling of distance from a sound source lowers the sound intensity level by 6 dB.

citations.title: Sleep in Middle and High School Students
citations.supports: Teens aged 13–18 should get 8 to 10 hours of sleep per 24 hours (American Academy of Sleep Medicine); about 7 in 10 high schoolers don't get enough on school nights; short sleep is linked to attention problems.

citations.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency: How Sleep Affects Your Health
citations.supports: During sleep the brain forms pathways to learn and remember; sleep-deficient people react more slowly, make more mistakes and have trouble focusing; ongoing sleep deficiency can weaken the body's defence against common infections.

limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Ringing that lasts more than a day, or hearing that stays muffled, is a reason to tell an adult.
